lines.text: From footraces at Olympia to World Cup finals watched by billions, this is the story of sport: the games, the clubs, and the legends who played them.
It begins in ancient Greece. Every four years athletes gathered at Olympia to honour Zeus, and warring cities agreed to lay down their arms while the games went on.
Watching over them sat a giant Zeus of ivory and gold, carved by Phidias. It stood for some eight hundred years before it was lost.
Centuries later, on the village greens of south-east England, a bat and ball game called cricket was taking shape. The empire would carry it around the world.
In 1787 the Marylebone Cricket Club was founded at Lord's in London. It wrote the Laws of Cricket, and it keeps them to this day.
Then came W. G. Grace, a bearded doctor with a bat, who ruled the Victorian game and turned cricket into a national passion.
In 1857 a club was formed in Sheffield that still plays today, the oldest football club in the world. It helped write the game's early rules.
Meanwhile a boy was born in Canada who would grow up to be a teacher, and give the world a new game: James Naismith.
In France, Pierre de Coubertin believed sport belonged in every education. He would found the Olympic committee and bring the ancient games back to life.
In 1863 football got its modern rules in England, splitting off from rugby. No team sport on Earth is played by more people.
Those rules were written by the Football Association, formed that year in a London pub. It still governs the English game and runs the FA Cup.
Up in Glasgow, Rangers was founded in 1872. Its rivalry with Celtic, the Old Firm, would become one of the fiercest in the game.
The next year, lawn tennis arrived in England, an outdoor cousin of much older indoor court games, played with rackets over a net.
By 1877 Wimbledon was under way on the grass of south-west London. It is the oldest tennis tournament in the world, and players still wear white.
In 1878 railway workers in Manchester started a team. It became Manchester United, a club that would rebuild after the Munich air disaster and win title after title.
Across the Atlantic, the US Open began in 1881. Today it closes the tennis summer on the hard courts of New York.
In 1882 Australia beat England on English soil, and a newspaper joked that English cricket had died. So began the Ashes, fought over a tiny urn ever since.
In 1886 workers at the royal arsenal in Woolwich formed a football team. Arsenal later moved north of the river, and once won the league without losing a game.
A year later a Catholic priest founded Celtic in Glasgow to help the poor. In 1967 it became the first British club to win the European Cup.
Jim Thorpe, a Native American athlete, would win gold in both the pentathlon and decathlon. His medals were stripped over amateur rules and restored only long after his death.
In 1891 the French championship began. Today, as the French Open on the red clay of Roland Garros, it is the hardest Grand Slam for most players to win.
That same winter in Massachusetts, Naismith hung up peach baskets so his students could play indoors. Basketball was born, and it would conquer the world.
In 1892 Liverpool was founded at Anfield. It would win league titles and European Cups, with its fans singing You'll Never Walk Alone.
In 1894, at a congress in Paris led by Coubertin, the International Olympic Committee was born. Its first task: games in Athens.
Around then Babe Ruth was born. He began as a pitcher, became baseball's great home run hitter with the Yankees, and made the sport a national craze.
In 1896 the modern Olympics opened in Athens, with men from a handful of nations. A Greek runner, Spyridon Louis, won the very first marathon.
In Turin, a group of schoolboys started a football club in 1897. Juventus, in black and white stripes, would become the most successful club in Italy.
Suzanne Lenglen of France would rule women's tennis in the twenties, its first true star.
In 1899 Joan Gamper and friends founded FC Barcelona. Owned by its members, it calls itself more than a club.
The same year, English expatriates founded AC Milan, a club that would lift the European Cup again and again.
In 1900 Bayern Munich was founded. It has won more German titles than anyone, and three European Cups in a row in the mid seventies.
Amsterdam's Ajax arrived that year too. Seventy years later, with Total Football and Johan Cruyff, it won three European Cups in a row.
The second Olympics, in Paris in 1900, sprawled over five months beside the World's Fair. For the first time, women competed.
That year also saw the first Davis Cup, tennis played nation against nation.
In 1902 Real Madrid was founded in the Spanish capital. Dressed in white, it would win the European Cup more than any other club.
That very year Madrid first met Barcelona. El Clasico grew into more than a match, carrying old rivalries between the capital and Catalonia.
In Lisbon, Benfica was founded in 1904. With Eusebio as its star, it would win two European Cups in the early sixties.
The same year, seven European countries met in Paris and founded FIFA. Today it has more than two hundred members and runs the World Cups.
The 1904 Olympics went to St. Louis, the first outside Europe. Few made the trip, but gold, silver and bronze were handed out for the first time.
In 1905, in the port district of Buenos Aires, Boca Juniors was born. Its battles with River Plate would become legendary.
Also in 1905 came the Australian championship, today the Grand Slam that opens every tennis year in Melbourne.
London hosted the Olympics in 1908. Its marathon ran from Windsor Castle to the stadium, and that distance became the standard ever since.
That year Don Bradman was born. His Test batting average of almost one hundred has never been matched, and many call him the greatest batsman ever.
In 1909 England, Australia and South Africa founded cricket's world body, which now runs its World Cups.
In Argentina, Juan Manuel Fangio was born. In the fifties he would win five world driving titles with four different teams.
Norway's Sonja Henie would glide to three Olympic golds and ten world titles, then become a Hollywood star.
In 1912 Santos was founded in Brazil. It became Pele's club, and in the early sixties it ruled the world of club football.
That summer's Stockholm Games drew athletes from all five inhabited continents, with electric timing and Jim Thorpe winning two golds.
Jesse Owens was born the next year. In Berlin he would win four golds in front of a regime that preached racial superiority.
In 1914 Brazil's national team played for the first time. In yellow shirts it would win five World Cups, more than anyone.
Fanny Blankers-Koen of the Netherlands would win four golds in 1948, a mother of two they called the Flying Housewife.
And Jackie Robinson was born in 1919. Decades later he broke baseball's colour line with the Brooklyn Dodgers, facing abuse with courage.
After the First World War, the Games went to battered Antwerp in 1920. The five-ring flag and the athletes' oath appeared there for the first time.
Emil Zatopek, the Czech Locomotive, would one day win the five thousand, the ten thousand and the marathon at a single Games.
In 1923 Wembley opened in London, with its famous twin towers. It would host the 1966 World Cup final.
In 1924 Chamonix in the French Alps staged skiing, skating, hockey and bobsleigh. These became known as the first Winter Olympics.
That summer Paris hosted again. Paavo Nurmi won five golds, British sprinters inspired Chariots of Fire, and athletes lived in the first Olympic Village.
In 1926 the Harlem Globetrotters started touring, dazzling crowds with trick shots and comedy and spreading basketball everywhere they went.
In Amsterdam in 1928 an Olympic flame burned above the stadium for the first time, and women competed in athletics and gymnastics.
In 1929 cars raced through the streets of Monte Carlo for the first time. The Monaco Grand Prix is still the most glamorous race of all.
The same year Ferrari's racing team was born. It is the only team to have raced in every Formula One season, and the most successful.
In 1930 Uruguay hosted the first football World Cup, with just thirteen teams, many arriving by ship. Uruguay beat Argentina to become champions.
The 1932 Olympics came to Los Angeles in the depths of the Depression. Winners stood on a podium for the first time.
Abebe Bikila was born in Ethiopia that year. He would win the Olympic marathon barefoot in Rome, then win it again in Tokyo.
Bill Russell would win eleven NBA titles with Boston, more than any player, and become the league's first Black head coach.
Italy hosted and won the second World Cup in 1934, the first with qualifying. Champions Uruguay stayed away.
Soviet gymnast Larisa Latynina would win eighteen Olympic medals, a record that stood for nearly half a century.
Scotland's Jim Clark would win two world titles with Lotus in the sixties, perhaps the most natural driver of his age.
In 1936 Nazi Germany used the Berlin Games to show off its power. Jesse Owens answered with four gold medals, and the torch relay was born.
Wilt Chamberlain, a towering centre, would one night in 1962 score one hundred points in a single game.
In 1938 Italy kept its World Cup in France. Then war came, and the tournament fell silent until 1950.
Australia's Rod Laver would twice win all four Grand Slams in a single year.
Wilma Rudolph beat childhood polio to win three golds in Rome, and became a star around the world and a voice for civil rights.
And in Brazil, Pele was born. At seventeen he played in a World Cup, and he would win three of them, scoring goals by the hundred.
Muhammad Ali won Olympic gold, then the heavyweight title three times. He refused to fight in Vietnam, and was banned from the ring for it.
Billie Jean King would win twelve Grand Slam titles and fight just as hard for equal prize money for women.
In 1946 a new professional league began. Renamed the NBA three years later, it would draw players from all over the world.
The Boston Celtics joined it that year. With Bill Russell they won eleven titles in thirteen seasons.
Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and his skyhook would make him the league's top scorer for decades.
Johan Cruyff, born in Amsterdam, would lead the Total Football of Ajax and the Netherlands, and later shape Barcelona as its coach.
The Lakers began in Minneapolis in 1947 and moved to Los Angeles in 1960, home to Magic Johnson and Kobe Bryant.
In 1948 a battered, rationed London hosted the first Games after the Second World War. They called them the Austerity Games.
Niki Lauda would win three Formula One titles, and come back from a terrible crash to race again.
For the 1950 World Cup, Brazil built the vast Maracana in Rio, which held almost two hundred thousand people.
There, in the deciding match, Uruguay stunned Brazil. The country still remembers it as the Maracanazo.
Also in 1950, the first Formula One world championship was raced, single-seaters on circuits around the globe.
Viv Richards of Antigua would lead the great West Indies sides, hitting the fastest bowlers without a helmet.
At the 1952 Games in Helsinki the Soviet Union took part for the first time, and Zatopek won three distance golds, including his very first marathon.
In 1954 West Germany beat mighty Hungary in the final in Bern. They called it the Miracle of Bern.
Alain Prost, The Professor, would win four world titles and fight a bitter rivalry with Senna.
In 1955 the European Cup began, gathering the continent's best clubs. Real Madrid won the first five.
Sweden's Bjorn Borg would win five Wimbledons in a row, ice cool against the fiery John McEnroe.
In 1956 a French magazine first named the best footballer of the year. The first Ballon d'Or went to Stanley Matthews.
Martina Navratilova, born in Czechoslovakia, would win eighteen Grand Slam singles titles, nine of them at Wimbledon.
Melbourne held the first Games in the southern hemisphere that year, shadowed by boycotts over Hungary and Suez.
Larry Bird would shoot the Celtics to three titles in the eighties, and win three MVP awards in a row.
In Sweden in 1958, a seventeen-year-old Pele scored in the final, and Brazil won its first World Cup.
Magic Johnson of the Lakers would duel with Bird all through the eighties, and together they revived the NBA.
Ayrton Senna would win three world titles for Brazil. His death at Imola in 1994 brought a whole nation to mourning.
The Rome Games of 1960 were the first shown on television in many countries. Bikila ran barefoot to marathon gold among the ancient ruins.
Soon after, Rome hosted several hundred wheelchair athletes, at what are counted as the first Paralympic Games.
Diego Maradona was born that year. He would captain Argentina to the 1986 World Cup and lead Napoli to its first titles.
In Canada came Wayne Gretzky, The Great One, who rewrote hockey's record book. His number ninety-nine is retired across the league.
Carl Lewis would win nine Olympic golds, including the long jump four Games in a row.
Romania's Nadia Comaneci would, at fourteen, score the first perfect ten in Olympic gymnastics.
In 1962 Chile hosted the World Cup two years after a great earthquake. With Pele injured, Garrincha led Brazil to a second straight title.
Michael Jordan was born the next year. He would win six titles with the Chicago Bulls and become one of the most famous athletes alive.
In 1963 Bruce McLaren founded his own racing team, which would become one of the most successful in Formula One.
In 1964 Tokyo hosted the first Olympics in Asia, showing off a rebuilt Japan, with the new bullet train opening just in time.
In 1966 England beat West Germany at Wembley in extra time to win its only World Cup, with a goal people still argue about.
In 1968 the Grand Slams opened their doors to professionals. Tennis became a game of prize money and television.
At the high-altitude Mexico City Games that year, records fell, and Tommie Smith and John Carlos raised gloved fists against racism.
Michael Schumacher was born in 1969. He would win seven world titles, five in a row with Ferrari.
Brian Lara of Trinidad would make the highest scores in Test and first-class cricket, four hundred and five hundred and one.
Steffi Graf would win all four Grand Slams and Olympic gold in one year, the Golden Slam.
Australia's Shane Warne would bring leg spin back to life, taking more than seven hundred Test wickets.
In Mexico in 1970, Pele's Brazil won a third title with a side many call the greatest ever. It was the first World Cup in colour.
Pete Sampras would win fourteen Grand Slams, seven of them at Wimbledon.
Sri Lanka's Muttiah Muralitharan would spin his way to more Test wickets than anyone in history.
Zinedine Zidane would lead France to the 1998 World Cup, then win three Champions Leagues as coach of Real Madrid.
The 1972 Munich Games were darkened when Palestinian gunmen took Israeli athletes hostage, and eleven Israelis were killed.
Ethiopia's Haile Gebrselassie would win two Olympic golds at ten thousand metres and set world record after world record.
In India, Sachin Tendulkar was born. Over almost a quarter of a century he would score more international runs than anyone.
In 1973 Billie Jean King beat Bobby Riggs before a huge television audience, a landmark for women in sport.
In 1974 West Germany won at home, beating Cruyff's Dutch, and lifted the golden trophy still used today.
In 1975 England hosted the first Cricket World Cup, and the West Indies won it.
Tiger Woods was born that year. He would win the Masters at twenty-one and take fifteen major titles.
At Montreal in 1976, Comaneci scored her perfect ten, most of Africa stayed away in protest, and the city paid off the bill for thirty years.
Argentina hosted in 1978 under military rule, and with two goals from Mario Kempes in the final, won its first World Cup.
Kobe Bryant would win five titles over twenty seasons with the Lakers, before his death in a helicopter crash in 2020.
In 1980 at Lake Placid, a team of American college players beat the mighty Soviets at hockey, in the middle of the Cold War.
That summer the United States and many others boycotted the Moscow Games over the invasion of Afghanistan.
Yao Ming would star for the Houston Rockets and make basketball a passion across China.
MS Dhoni, calm as ever behind the stumps, would lead India to world titles in both the short and long white-ball games.
Roger Federer was born in 1981. With his smooth style he would win twenty Grand Slams and spend over three hundred weeks at number one.
The same year came Serena Williams, who would win twenty-three Grand Slam singles titles, the most of the open era.
In Spain in 1982, the first World Cup with twenty-four teams, Paolo Rossi's goals carried Italy to its third title.
In 1983 India, the outsiders under Kapil Dev, beat the mighty West Indies at Lord's. Cricket became India's great passion.
The 1984 Los Angeles Games, paid for largely by sponsors, made a profit and changed how cities saw hosting. Most of the Soviet bloc stayed home.
Kenya's Eliud Kipchoge would win two Olympic marathons, and in 2019 run the distance in under two hours.
LeBron James would win four titles with three teams, and pass Kareem as the NBA's all-time top scorer.
Lewis Hamilton was born in 1985. He would win seven world titles and more Formula One races than anyone.
That year also brought Cristiano Ronaldo, one of the highest scorers ever, who led Portugal to the 2016 European title.
And Michael Phelps, who would win twenty-eight Olympic medals, eight golds in Beijing alone.
In Mexico in 1986, Maradona scored twice against England, once with his hand and once after a dribble past half the team, and Argentina won.
Rafael Nadal would win the French Open fourteen times, and twenty-two Grand Slams in all.
Jamaica's Usain Bolt would set world records in the hundred and two hundred metres, and win eight Olympic golds.
Serbia's Novak Djokovic would go further still, with more men's Grand Slam titles and weeks at number one than anyone.
Lionel Messi was born that year too. He would win the Ballon d'Or more than anyone, and the World Cup in 2022.
Sebastian Vettel would win four world titles in a row with Red Bull.
Stephen Curry would change basketball with his long three-point shots, and win four titles with Golden State.
The 1988 Seoul Games were the first in years without a big boycott, drawing over a hundred and fifty nations.
Virat Kohli would score more than eighty international hundreds, and become one of the most followed sportsmen on Earth.
In 1989 a crush at Hillsborough in Sheffield killed many football fans. Their families' long fight for justice changed stadiums for good.
West Germany won a cautious World Cup in Italy in 1990, and the rules were changed to make the game more attacking.
In 1991 China hosted the first Women's World Cup, won by the United States. It has grown ever since.
The next year England's top clubs broke away to form the Premier League. Huge television deals made it the richest league in the world.
That summer the Dream Team of NBA stars took gold in Barcelona and spread basketball across the globe.
Barcelona's Games came just after the Cold War ended, bringing almost every nation together and renewing the city.
In 1994 at Imola, Roland Ratzenberger and Ayrton Senna were killed in one weekend, and the sport pushed hard for safety.
That summer the United States hosted a record-breaking World Cup, and Brazil beat Italy in the first final settled on penalties.
Shohei Ohtani, born that year in Japan, would pitch and hit at the top level, something not seen since Babe Ruth.
In 1996 the WNBA was founded, giving women a professional basketball league of their own.
At the centennial Games in Atlanta, Muhammad Ali lit the flame, and Michael Johnson won both the two hundred and four hundred metres.
Simone Biles would win more world medals than any gymnast, with moves so hard they carry her name.
Max Verstappen would win four Formula One titles in a row from 2021.
In 1998 France hosted the first World Cup of thirty-two teams, and Zidane's two headers beat Brazil in the final.
Kylian Mbappe, born that year, would win the World Cup at nineteen and score a hat-trick in another final.
At Sydney in 2000, Cathy Freeman lit the flame and won the four hundred metres, and the two Koreas marched together.
Italy's Jannik Sinner would reach number one in 2024, in a fierce new rivalry with Carlos Alcaraz.
Japan and South Korea shared the first World Cup in Asia in 2002. Brazil won a fifth title, and South Korea reached the semi-finals.
Spain's Carlos Alcaraz would become the youngest man ever ranked number one, at just nineteen.
In 2004 the Olympics came home to Athens, the shot put was held at ancient Olympia, and Phelps won six golds.
Red Bull Racing entered Formula One in 2005, and would win titles with Vettel and later Verstappen.
Germany hosted a joyful World Cup in 2006, and Italy won it on penalties in Berlin.
In 2007 cricket held its first world championship of the short twenty-over game, and India won it.
A year later the Indian Premier League began, city teams in a twenty-over league that became the richest in cricket.
Beijing's 2008 Games opened in the Bird's Nest. Phelps won eight golds, and Bolt set world records in both sprints.
In 2010 South Africa hosted the first World Cup in Africa, filled with vuvuzelas, and Spain won its first title.
That year Mercedes returned with its own team, and from 2014 it won eight constructors' titles in a row.
In 2012 London hosted for a third time, and for the first time every nation sent women athletes.
In Brazil in 2014, Germany crushed the hosts seven goals to one in the semi-final, then beat Argentina to win the cup.
In 2016 Rio de Janeiro hosted the first Olympics in South America.
In Russia in 2018, referees used video review for the first time, and France beat Croatia to win its second title.
The Tokyo Games were put off a year by the pandemic, and held in 2021 in almost empty stadiums.
In Qatar in 2022, Messi's Argentina beat France on penalties, in a final many call the greatest ever.
In 2024 Paris opened its Games with a parade of boats along the Seine, a century after it last hosted.
In 2026 Milan and Cortina shared the Winter Games, the first Olympics officially held by two cities.
And that summer the United States, Canada and Mexico hosted forty-eight teams. Spain won, its second World Cup.
From Olympia to the world's stadiums, the games go on, and new legends are always waiting.
